claim: Trump's 9 Jul 2025 letter to Lula announced a 50% tariff on all Brazilian goods from 1 Aug 2025, called the Bolsonaro trial "a Witch Hunt that should end IMMEDIATELY" and ordered a Section 301 probe.

EO 14323 of 30 Jul 2025 imposed an additional 40% ad valorem duty on Brazilian goods effective 6 Aug 2025, on top of the 10% reciprocal baseline (50% total); goods in transit before 6 Aug and entered by 5 Oct 2025 were exempt.
Annex I of the 30 Jul 2025 order exempted 694 products from the 40% (incl. civil aircraft and parts, orange juice/pulp, petroleum and fuels, wood pulp, iron ore, fertilizers).

MDIC computed that the 50% surcharge hit 35.9% of Brazil's exports to the US (US$14.5bn in 2024), 44.6% were outside the 40% add-on, and 19.5% (US$7.9bn) were under Section 232 sectoral tariffs; Amcham put exemptions at 43.4% (US$18.4bn of US$42.3bn).

In 2025 the drop in Brazil's US exports was driven mainly by crude oil (-30.4%) and semi-finished iron/steel (-21.7%); the US share of Brazil's exports fell from 12.0% (2024) to 10.8% (2025); H1-2026 sales were US$17.4bn (-13% y/y).
The US Supreme Court ruled 6–3 in Learning Resources v. Trump (20 Feb 2026) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, voiding the IEEPA-based 10%+40% Brazil tariffs.

MDIC (24 Feb 2026): under the post-ruling regime, 46% of Brazil's US exports (US$17.5bn) faced no additional tariff, ~25% (US$9.3bn) the Section 122 rate, and 29% (US$10.9bn) Section 232 tariffs.

The USTR Section 301 probe of Brazil, opened 15 Jul 2025 (FR notice 18 Jul, docket USTR-2025-0043), covered digital trade and electronic payment services (incl. Pix), preferential tariffs, anti-corruption, IP, ethanol market access and illegal deforestation.

USTR determined on 1 Jun 2026 that Brazil's practices are unreasonable and actionable under Section 301, and proposed a 25% tariff with over 1,600 product categories exempted (incl. petroleum, coffee, beef, orange juice, civil aircraft).

USTR's final Section 301 action (15 Jul 2026) imposed an additional 25% on most Brazilian goods from 22 Jul 2026; goods under Section 232 are excluded; exemptions include beef, coffee, orange juice, aircraft and parts, energy, pig iron.
A separate Section 301 forced-labor action on 60 economies added 12.5% on Brazil (the top rate) from 24 Jul 2026, stacking with the 25% for a combined 37.5% on covered goods.

MDIC (24 Jul 2026, 2024 base of US$40.4bn): 16.5% of Brazil's US exports (US$6.6bn: machinery, wood, oils, footwear, furniture, apparel) face 37.5%; 52.7% (US$21.3bn: coffee, meat, pig iron, aircraft, OJ, fruit, most pulp) are exempt; 24.2% (US$9.8bn) are under Section 232.

Global Trade Alert estimates the final 301 action fully hits US$8.5bn of US$39.6bn 2024 US imports from Brazil (US$20.1bn exempt, US$7.3bn Section 232), raising the trade-weighted US tariff on Brazil from 11.0% to 17.5% (17.7% with forced-labor), or ~US$7.0bn/yr in duties.
